1	# Silmulator — Glossary
2	
3	Terms the learner has demonstrably grasped are added here.
4	
5	| Term | Definition |
6	|------|------------|
7	| ConnectionPort | A `QGraphicsEllipseItem` child of a block that holds `port_id`, `parent_block`, and `connected_to` (the peer port, or None). Coloured blue when free, green when connected. |
8	| WireItem | A `QGraphicsLineItem` in the scene (not a child of any block) that draws a gold line between two ConnectionPorts. ZValue = -1 so blocks render above it. |
9	| x_frac / y_frac | Fractional coordinates (0.0–1.0) passed to `add_port()` that are multiplied by the block's BLOCK_WIDTH / BLOCK_HEIGHT to position a port in local coordinates. |
10	| hardware_docs/ | The folder in the repo where vendor PDFs, SCPI command tables, and notes are stored. Not auto-parsed; feeds the custom-block authoring workflow. |
11	| custom block spec | A JSON file in `silmulator/custom_blocks/` that declares a block's name, colour, port layout, and SCPI command map. Loaded at startup by `discover_specs()`. |
12	| SIL | Software-in-the-Loop: both the controller logic and the instruments are simulated in software. No real hardware. |
13	| HIL | Hardware-in-the-Loop: the real embedded controller runs in real time; only the instruments/plant are simulated. |
14	| CIL | Code-in-the-Loop: actual source files are the artifact under test; SCPI calls extracted from them are replayed against simulated instruments. The Code Input block enables this. |
15	| SCPI | Standard Commands for Programmable Instruments (IEEE 488.2). A tree-structured text command language used by lab instruments and simulated here. |
16	| reference voltage | The voltage pair (VR+/VR−) an ADC compares its input against — the conversion's unit of measure. In the MSP430 model, `_adc_reference_voltage()` resolves VR+ from the selected `ADC:REFERENCE` (AVCC live via `clock.vcc`, REF_A outputs, or VeREF+); VR− is fixed at AVSS (0 V). |
17	| full-scale code | The maximum ADC output, 2^resolution − 1 (4095/1023/255). Produced when Vin ≥ VR+, so it means "at or above the reference" — possibly clipping — never a specific voltage. Clamped in `FaultState.adc_code()`. |
18	| transfer function | The input→code mapping NADC = FS × (Vin − VR−)/(VR+ − VR−) (SLAU367P §34.2.1 Eq. 13). An ADC code is a ratio of the reference span, not a voltage. Implemented as `int(voltage / full_scale_v * max_code)`, clamped. |
19	| LSB voltage | The input-voltage width of one code step: (VR+ − VR−)/FS. ≈293 µV under the 1.2-V VREF vs ≈806 µV under 3.3-V AVCC at 12 bits — the reference sets granularity as well as range. |
20	| ADC12VRSEL | The 4-bit ADC12MCTLx field (SLAU367P §34.2.4) selecting which physical sources drive VR+/VR−. A finite register encoding — mirrored by `VALID_ADC_REFERENCES`, which is why `ADC:REFERENCE BANANA` is rejected with SCPI -224. |
21	| REF_A | The FR5994's shared internal reference module (SLAU367P §33): bandgap-derived 1.2/2.0/2.5-V outputs selected by REFVSEL (reset default 00b = 1.2 V). Modelled by the `ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V` dict; bare `VREF` maps to the reset default. |
22	| VeREF+ | The external positive-reference pin (SLASE54D Table 7-1) — board-supplied, no defined reset state. Modelled as `_veref_v`, set via `ADC:REFERENCE VEREF,<v>` (non-numeric voltage → SCPI -104), reset to 1.2 by `*RST`. |
23	| ratiometric measurement | Referencing the ADC to the same source that powers the sensor so the supply cancels: N = FS × (k·AVCC)/AVCC = FS × k. The reason AVCC exists as a reference choice; testable because AVCC reads `clock.vcc` live at conversion time. |
24	| register width | The number of physical flip-flops in a register, fixing its representable values at 0 … 2^width − 1. TAxR/TAxCCRn are 16-bit; writes outside 0–0xFFFF are rejected with SCPI -222 (`_timer_count`, `_timer_cc_val`). Python ints are unbounded, so the model must enforce width explicitly. |
25	| encoding | The finite mapping from a register field's bit patterns to behaviours — an n-bit field reaches at most 2^n values. The timer divider is ID (2 bits) × TAIDEX (3 bits), max /64; /128 has no encoding and draws -224. Width bounds magnitude; encoding bounds meaning. |
26	| reachable state space | The set of states real hardware can occupy — the closure of all field encodings. A simulator's accepted inputs must stay inside it: accepting an unreachable state (the old /128) silently voids every downstream SIL result. The accepted set may be a documented *subset* (the power-of-two dividers). |
27	| write masking | Truncating an over-width write to the register width (`value & 0xFFFF`) instead of refusing it — what a 16-bit bus does physically. Silmulator rejects with -222 instead; `test_count_over_16bit_rejected_or_masked` blesses either policy, forbidding only verbatim storage. |
28	| TAIDEX | The 3-bit input divider expansion field in TAxEX0 (÷1…8), cascaded after ID (÷1/2/4/8) in TAxCTL. Effective divider = ID × TAIDEX product: 20 reachable values, max 8×8 = /64 — why `TIMERA0:CLOCK:DIVIDER 128` is impossible and rejected. |
29	| CAP bit | The per-CC-unit mode bit in TAxCCTLn: compare (CCRn holds a written value) vs capture (an edge latches the count into CCRn). Stored state since a20fbb1 (`cc_mode` dict, -224 validation); capture *events* are out of scope — time does not pass. |
30	| register aliasing | Two interface names denoting one physical register, modeled as delegation to a single store. PERIOD IS TAxCCR0 (SLAU367P §25.2.3.1): `_timer_period` is `return self._timer_cc_val(cmd, ts, 0)` — the old independent `period` field was the double-store bug class. |
31	| stored-state modeling | Simulating a device as a validated state machine with no autonomous dynamics: registers hold what was written; counting, latching, and interrupts never happen because time does not pass. Model configuration fully, document dynamics as out of scope — never fake them. |

ADC Reference Transfer Functions — Vocabulary

Eight terms behind the reference-aware ADC conversion. Each has a definition, a project example from the real code, a usage sentence, and a contrast with the term it's most often confused with.

Reference voltage (VR+ / VR−)

89
the conversion's unit of measure
90
91
Definition
92
The voltage pair an ADC compares its input against: VR+ maps to the full-scale code, VR− maps to code 0. Every output code is a fraction of the span between them — the reference literally defines what one "unit" of the result means. Change the reference and the same physical input produces a different code.
93
Project example
94
In silmulator/devices/msp430.py, _adc_reference_voltage() resolves VR+ at conversion time — clock.vcc for AVCC, _veref_v for VEREF, or an ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V lookup for REF_A's outputs. VR− is fixed at AVSS (0 V) in this model. Before commit 58b7e2d, this function didn't exist and VR+ was a hardcoded 3.3.
95
Usage
96
"The RAW code looks huge because you left the 1.2-V reference voltage selected — 1.2 V in, 1.2 V reference, full scale out."
97
Contrast with: supply voltage
98
The supply (AVCC) powers the chip; the reference calibrates the measurement. They coincide only when AVCC is selected as the reference — and then supply drift becomes measurement drift, which is exactly what CPU:VCC 3.0 now lets a SIL test exercise.

Full-scale code (FS)

105
4095 · 1023 · 255
106
107
Definition
108
The maximum code an ADC can output: 2resolution − 1. It is produced when Vin ≥ VR+, so reading it means "at or above the reference" — possibly clipping — never a specific voltage.
109
Project example
110
msp430_faults.py computes max_code = (1 << resolution) - 1 and clamps with max(0, min(max_code, code)). The audit probe adc_ignores_reference asserts that 1.2 V against the 1.2-V VREF returns exactly 4095 — the input equals the reference, so the result is full scale.
111
Usage
112
"Inject 2.5 V against VREF2.0 and you'll read the full-scale code — the ideal 5118 clips to 4095."
113
Contrast with: full-scale voltage
114
The full-scale code is fixed by ADC:RESOLUTION (ADC12RES); the full-scale voltage is whatever reference is selected. Switching VREF2.5 → AVCC moves the voltage that produces 4095 from 2.5 V to 3.3 V, but 4095 itself never changes.

Transfer function

SLAU367P §34.2.1, Equation 13
122
123
Definition
124
The mapping from analog input to digital output code: NADC = FS × (Vin − VR−) / (VR+ − VR−), quantised and clamped. It makes explicit that an ADC code is a ratio of the reference span, not a voltage.
125
Project example
126
Implemented in FaultState.adc_code(): int(voltage / full_scale_v * max_code) with VR− = 0. Commit 58b7e2d's whole point was feeding the correct full_scale_v (the selected reference) into this function instead of the literal 3.3 — the CORNER profile then layers gain/offset/INL errors on top of the same ideal transfer curve.
127
Usage
128
"Work the transfer function forward to predict the code, and backward to recover volts — with the same reference both ways, or you get commit-58b7e2d's bug class."
129
Contrast with: calibration curve
130
The transfer function is the ideal, datasheet-defined mapping. A calibration curve characterises how a particular part deviates from it (gain, offset, INL — what the simulator's CORNER fault profile injects). You design against the transfer function; you correct against a calibration.

The input-voltage width of one code step — the smallest voltage change the conversion can resolve. Set jointly by the reference span and the resolution: shrink the reference or raise the resolution, and each code is worth fewer microvolts.

Project example
142
With the references Silmulator now honours: 1.2 V / 4095 ≈ 293 µV per LSB under VREF, versus 3.3 V / 4095 ≈ 806 µV under default AVCC. The CORNER profile's INL spec is quoted in these units — a ±2.2-LSB bow in msp430_faults.py — which is only meaningful once you know the LSB's voltage value.

"Reading a 0–1 V sensor against AVCC wastes resolution — switch to VREF1.2 and your LSB voltage drops from 806 µV to 293 µV."

Resolution is the number of steps (12-bit → 4096 of them); LSB voltage is how many volts each step spans. ADC:RESOLUTION changes the step count; ADC:REFERENCE changes the step size. Both knobs move the LSB voltage, only one moves the code range.

The 4-bit field in the MSP430's ADC12MCTLx conversion-memory registers that selects which physical sources drive VR+ and VR−. Because it is a register field, the set of possible references is finite and fixed by silicon — there is no encoding for an arbitrary voltage.

1. Protection by Reset — Why a Wrong Password Reboots the Chip

The watchdog exists to catch runaway code: a corrupted program counter, a wild pointer, a stack smash — anything that sends the CPU executing garbage. The one thing runaway code must never be able to do is silently disable the mechanism that catches runaway code.

So TI puts a lock on the door. Every write to WDTCTL — the watchdog's control register — must carry the password 0x5A in its upper byte (SLAU367P §24.2, the WDTPW field). And here is the crucial design decision: a write with the wrong password does not fail with an error flag. It triggers an immediate PUC — a power-up clear, a reset.

💡 The mental model
Think about what runaway code looks like from the register file's point of view: a stream of essentially random writes spraying across the address space. The probability that a random 16-bit write to WDTCTL happens to carry 0x5A in its upper byte is 1 in 256. Any of the other 255 patterns doesn't just get rejected — it reboots the chip into a known-good state. The failure mode of the protection is recovery. That is protection by reset.

Contrast the two philosophies:

DesignWrong write to a safety registerWhat runaway code experiences
Error codeStatus flag set; write ignoredNothing — garbage code never checks status flags. It keeps running, and may eventually hit the bit pattern that disables the watchdog.
Protection by reset (MSP430)Immediate PUCExecution ends now. PC reloads from the reset vector, peripherals return to defaults, the watchdog restarts. The system is back in a state the firmware author designed for.

The same pattern guards other critical MSP430 registers: the clock system (CSCTL0 wants password 0xA5), FRAM control, and the PMM all use password fields, and violations cause resets. WDTCTL is the canonical example because the watchdog is the register a fault would most "want" to disable.

2. WDTCTL Anatomy — WDTPW in the Upper Byte, WDTHOLD at Bit 7

WDTCTL is a 16-bit register (SLAU367P §24.2, Figure 24-2). The layout that matters here:

15        WDTPW = 0x5A        8 | 7 HOLD | 6 … 0  SSEL/TMSEL/CNTCL/IS… bits 15–8: write password (reads return 0x69 on real silicon); bit 7: WDTHOLD (1 = watchdog stopped); bits 6–0: clock select, mode, counter clear, interval select

Silmulator mirrors exactly the two fields it models, as named class constants:

# silmulator/silmulator/devices/msp430.py — added by 5e2ba08
# WDTCTL (SLAU367P §24.2, Figure 24-2): bits 15-8 are the write password
# (WDTPW, must be 0x5A), bit 7 is WDTHOLD.
WDT_PASSWORD = 0x5A
WDT_HOLD_BIT = 0x80

Worked example 1 — the canonical "stop the watchdog" write

Every MSP430 hello-world starts with WDTCTL = WDTPW | WDTHOLD;, i.e. 0x5A80:

value            = 0x5A80
value >> 8       = 0x5A          # upper byte — matches WDT_PASSWORD ✓
value & 0x80     = 0x80 → truthy # bit 7 set → wdt.hold = True (stopped)

Worked example 2 — correct password, watchdog left running

value            = 0x5A00
value >> 8       = 0x5A          # password ✓ — write accepted
value & 0x80     = 0x00 → falsy  # bit 7 clear → wdt.hold = False (started)

Worked example 3 — the violation

value            = 0x1234
value >> 8       = 0x12 ≠ 0x5A   # password ✗ → immediate PUC

Worked example 4 — the trap: right bits, wrong byte

value            = 0xA55A        # 0x5A is in the LOWER byte
value >> 8       = 0xA5 ≠ 0x5A   # password ✗ → PUC. (0xA5 is CSCTL0's
                                 # password — wrong lock, wrong door.)
⚠ Bit 7, not "any nonzero low byte"
WDT:PASSWORD 0x5A08 is accepted (password is right) but 0x08 & 0x80 = 0, so the watchdog is started, not held. On real silicon 0x08 is WDTCNTCL territory. Only bit 7 is WDTHOLD — the model tests exactly that bit: bool(value & self.WDT_HOLD_BIT).

One more subtlety from the real part: reads of WDTCTL return 0x69 in the upper byte, not 0x5A — so firmware that does a read-modify-write of WDTCTL must overwrite the upper byte with 0x5A or it will reset itself. The simulator doesn't expose a WDTCTL read, but this is why the password is called a write password.

3. The Fix — What Commit 5e2ba08 Actually Changed

The MSP430 compliance audit scored both WDT families NON_COMPLIANT: "WDT:PASSWORD — No-op. Real WDTCTL writes need 0x5A in the upper byte and a wrong password causes an immediate PUC — the model accepts anything silently." And WDT:STATE? always answered RUNNING regardless of writes.

Before: both handlers were stubs

# silmulator/silmulator/devices/msp430.py — BEFORE 5e2ba08
def _wdt_state(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
    if cmd.is_query:
        return "RUNNING"       # constant — writes silently ignored
    return ""

def _wdt_password(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
    return ""                  # any password "succeeds" — no check, no PUC

After: real stored state and a real PUC path

# AFTER 5e2ba08 — new dataclass
@dataclass
class WDTState:
    """WDT_A control state (SLAU367P §24.2, WDTCTL).

    ``hold`` mirrors WDTHOLD (bit 7): 0 = watchdog started/running (the PUC
    default), 1 = held/stopped. No interval countdown is modeled — time does
    not pass in this simulation — so the watchdog never expires on its own;
    only a password violation on a WDTCTL-style write causes a PUC.
    """
    hold: bool = False
def _wdt_password(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
    """WDT:PASSWORD <value> — emulated WDTCTL write (SLAU367P §24.2, WDTPW)."""
    if not cmd.params:
        raise ScpiError(-109, "Missing parameter: password value")
    value = int(cmd.params[0], 0) & 0xFFFF       # 16-bit register width
    if (value >> 8) != self.WDT_PASSWORD:
        self._do_reset()  # wrong password: immediate PUC
        return ""
    self.wdt.hold = bool(value & self.WDT_HOLD_BIT)
    return ""

Read that violation branch carefully — three deliberate choices:

  • It calls self._do_reset() — the same shared reset path that *RST uses. A PUC is not a special WDT-only event; it resets the whole device: all peripherals rebuilt, memory cleared, PC reloaded from the reset vector, GIE cleared. The audit's *RST row was updated to say exactly this: "Restores simulator defaults via the same _do_reset path a WDT password violation PUC uses, including WDTHOLD."
  • It does not raise ScpiError — a PUC is a hardware event, not a command error. The test asserts errors(mcu) == 0 after the violation.
  • It returns normally — from the SCPI client's perspective the write "succeeded"; the evidence is the device state afterwards, exactly like probing real hardware.

The regression test — read what a PUC destroys

# tests/test_msp430_edge_cases.py — added by 5e2ba08
def test_wrong_password_causes_puc(self, mcu):
    mcu.process("CPU:PC 0x8000")
    mcu.process("GPIO:PORT1:OUTPUT 0xFF")
    mcu.process("WDT:STATE HOLD")
    mcu.process("WDT:PASSWORD 0x1234")  # 0x12 != 0x5A
    assert mcu._pc == mcu._reset_vector_pc()  # PC went to the reset vector
    assert mcu.ports[1].output == 0x00        # peripheral state also reset
    assert mcu.wdt.hold is False               # WDT itself reset to its default
    assert errors(mcu) == 0                    # PUC is a hardware event, not a SCPI error

Note the setup: the test deliberately dirties three unrelated pieces of state (PC, a GPIO port, the WDT hold bit) and then verifies all three were wiped. That is what distinguishes "a PUC happened" from "the write was ignored."

def _wdt_state(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:

4. BOR → POR → PUC — The Reset Hierarchy, and the Shared Reset Path

"PUC" is the mildest of three nested reset levels the MSP430 defines (SLAU367P §1.2). Each deeper level triggers everything below it:

LevelNameTypical causesAlso triggers
BORBrownout resetPowering the device up; supply falling below the brownout threshold; RST/NMI pin (reset mode); software via PMMSWBORPOR, PUC
PORPower-on resetA BOR; security violation; software via PMMSWPORPUC
PUCPower-up clearA POR; watchdog expiry (watchdog mode); WDT password violation; FRAM/CS/PMM register password violations; fetch from vacant memory—

Notice the pattern in the PUC row: apart from "a POR happened," every PUC source is a symptom of broken software — the dog timed out, a protected register got a garbage write, the CPU wandered into empty address space. A PUC is the hardware saying "the program has lost its mind; restart it." What a PUC does:

  • PC is loaded from the reset vector at 0xFFFE — the top entry of the FR5994 vector table (SLASE54D Table 9-4, priority 63, "highest").
  • The status register is cleared — including GIE, so interrupts are masked until the firmware re-enables them.
  • Peripheral registers return to their documented reset values — including WDTHOLD = 0: the watchdog wakes up running. Firmware that doesn't pet or stop it promptly gets a second PUC ~32 ms later.

How Silmulator models it: one shared _do_reset()

# msp430.py — the single reset path (*RST, and now WDT password violations)
def _do_reset(self) -> None:
    self.ports   = {i: GPIOPort()   for i in range(1, self.NUM_PORTS + 1)}
    self.adc     = {i: ADCChannel() for i in range(self.NUM_ADC_CH)}
    # … timers, UART, SPI, I2C, clock, PM all rebuilt …
    self.wdt     = WDTState()          # hold=False — watchdog RUNNING again
    self._veref_v = 1.2
    self._memory = {}
    self._pc = self._reset_vector_pc() # PC ← reset vector
    self._registers = [0] * 16
    self._gie = False  # SR.GIE is cleared on a PUC (SLAU367P §4.3.3)
def _reset_vector_pc(self) -> int:
    """PC on reset (SLAU367P §4.3, §1.2): fetched from the reset vector at
    0xFFFE/0xFFFF (little-endian word). Defaults to 0x4000 — FRAM code
    start (SLASE54D memory map) — when the vector has not been written."""
    lo = self._memory.get(0xFFFE)
    hi = self._memory.get(0xFFFF)
    if lo is None and hi is None:
        return 0x4000
    return ((hi or 0) << 8) | (lo or 0)

Worked example — where does the PC land?

CPU:PC 0x8000                 # firmware "running" at 0x8000
WDT:PASSWORD 0x1234           # 0x12 ≠ 0x5A → _do_reset()

Inside _do_reset:
  self._memory = {}           # memory wiped FIRST…
  _reset_vector_pc():
    _memory.get(0xFFFE) → None
    _memory.get(0xFFFF) → None
    → 0x4000                  # …so the vector is unwritten → FRAM default

PC after the violation = 0x4000  (not 0x8000, not 0xFFFE)
⚠ 0xFFFE is where the vector LIVES, not where the PC goes
The reset vector is a pointer stored at 0xFFFE/0xFFFF. The PC is loaded with the pointer's value. In the simulator, _do_reset clears _memory before reading the vector, so post-PUC the PC is always the 0x4000 FRAM-start default. (A real PUC does not erase FRAM — this is a modeling simplification worth knowing when you write assertions.)

One deliberate divergence to keep in mind: the simulator collapses BOR, POR and PUC into the single _do_reset path. It models the consequences of a PUC (state wiped, PC at the vector, GIE clear, watchdog running), not the three-tier cause machinery.

5. The Same Trust Boundary on the Bus — I2C NACKs Unknown Addresses (fa7c595)

Issue #23's I2C commit applies the same philosophy one layer out: the world must be allowed to say no. Before fa7c595, every I2C write returned ACK and I2Cn:TRANSFER parsed a target address and then ignored it — every address behaved identically, so firmware talking to a sensor that wasn't there could never find out.

Per-address routing with a NACK path

# I2CState — after fa7c595
address: int = 0x50
address_10bit: bool = False   # UCSLA10/UCA10 (SLAU367P §32.3.1)
# Per-address rx/tx queues: one simulated slave per populated address.
# An address with no entry has no device present and NACKs (UCNACKIFG).
addr_buffers: Dict[int, Dict[str, List[int]]] = field(
    default_factory=lambda: {0x50: {"rx": [], "tx": []}}
)
# _i2c_transfer — the routing decision
addr = int(cmd.params[0], 0)
if addr not in ii.addr_buffers:
    return "NACK"              # no simulated device lives there
buf = ii.addr_buffers[addr]        # independent queue per slave
buf["tx"].extend(data)
response = bytes(buf["rx"][:len(data)])

Worked example, straight from the updated audit probe:

I2C0:TRANSFER 0x50,"AB"   → "00"    # 0x50 is the pre-registered default slave;
                                    # rx queue empty → zero-fill, 1 byte → "00"
I2C0:TRANSFER 0x77,"AB"   → "NACK"  # nobody registered 0x77 → the bus says no

A slave comes into existence two ways: configuring it (I2C0:ADDRESS 0x29 calls addr_buffers.setdefault(0x29, …)) or an addressed injection (inject_i2c_rx(0, data, address=0x29)) — the test harness placing a simulated device on the bus.

Validation replaced silent truncation

# BEFORE: ii.address = int(cmd.params[0], 0) & 0x7F
#   I2C0:ADDRESS 0x80  →  0x80 & 0x7F = 0x00 — silently became address 0!
# AFTER:
limit = 0x3FF if mode_10bit else 0x7F
if not 0 <= addr <= limit:
    raise ScpiError(-222, f"I2C address out of range for {width} mode (0-0x{limit:X})")
  • 7-bit mode (default, UCSLA10 = 0): addresses 0–0x7F. I2C0:ADDRESS 0x80 → -222.
  • 10-bit mode (I2C0:ADDRESS 0x2FF,10BIT): addresses 0–0x3FF; the query echoes 0x2FF in three hex digits.
  • Frequency: the old handler had a dead if v not in (100000, 400000, 1000000): pass branch. Now anything but the three real eUSCI_B modes (100 kHz standard / 400 kHz fast / 1 MHz fast-plus) raises -222.
💡 Same idea, different mechanisms
WDTCTL protects with a reset; the I2C bus protects with a NACK; a register field protects with -224/-222. In every case the fix is the same shape: the old model always said yes, and a simulator that always says yes can never expose firmware that fails to handle "no."

6. Interrupt State That Is Real but Minimal — GIE and Table 9-4 (615b4e1)

The third commit gives the interrupt system genuine stored state without pretending time passes:

  • GIE is real: self._gie models SR bit 3 (SLAU367P §4.3.3). INTERRUPT:ENABLE / DISABLE mirror EINT / DINT; INTERRUPT:GIE ON|OFF sets it directly; a PUC clears it (self._gie = False in _do_reset — tying section 4 back in).
  • Vectors are the real Table 9-4 word addresses, in the real priority order, for the sources the model tracks enable+flag state for:
# SLASE54D Table 9-4, highest → lowest priority (modeled sources only)
_TIMERB_VECTOR = 0xFFF4                                  # TB0IV
_TIMERA_VECTORS = {0: 0xFFE8, 1: 0xFFE0, 2: 0xFFDA}     # TAxIV
_GPIO_PORT_VECTORS = {1: 0xFFDE, 2: 0xFFD8, 3: 0xFFD2, 4: 0xFFD0,
                      5: 0xFFC6, 6: 0xFFC4, 7: 0xFFB8, 8: 0xFFB6}
_INTERRUPT_PRIORITY = ("TB0","TA0","TA1","P1","TA2","P2","P3","P4","P5","P6","P7","P8")

The two queries deliberately disagree about GIE

GPIO:PORT1:INTERRUPT:ENABLE 0x01   # P1IE bit 0
GPIO:PORT1:INTERRUPT:FLAG 0x01     # P1IFG bit 0 — pending!

INTERRUPT:VECTOR?  → 0x0000        # GIE clear: no maskable interrupt would be taken
INTERRUPT:FLAG?    → 1             # IFG bits are set REGARDLESS of GIE

INTERRUPT:GIE ON
INTERRUPT:VECTOR?  → 0xFFDE        # P1's real Table 9-4 word address

That split matches silicon: an IFG flag latches whether or not interrupts are enabled; GIE only gates whether the CPU services it. And priority is honored: if TA0 (0xFFE8) and P1 (0xFFDE) are both pending, VECTOR? reports 0xFFE8 — _pending_interrupt_vector() walks _INTERRUPT_PRIORITY in order and returns the first hit, else 0x0000 (mirroring an IV register reading 0 when nothing is pending — no vector in Table 9-4 is address 0).

What is deliberately absent: flags never fire on their own (no timer ever rolls over — time does not pass), no ISR is ever "entered," and every untracked Table 9-4 row (WDT, eUSCI, ADC12_B, DMA, RTC_C, AES, Comp_E, LEA, the NMIs) never contributes a vector. The audit calls this minimal wiring: configuration and pending-state are real; dynamics are out of scope — the same stored-state honesty as the watchdog that never expires.

7. Often Confused

ConfusionThe distinction
"A wrong password is rejected with an error" No — it triggers a PUC. The device state after WDT:PASSWORD 0x1234 is a freshly reset device with an empty error queue (errors(mcu) == 0). Rejection-with-error is the -224/-222 pattern for configuration registers; safety registers protect by reset.
PUC vs POR vs BOR Three nested levels (SLAU367P §1.2). BOR is deepest (power-up, supply droop) and triggers POR, which triggers PUC. A watchdog event or password violation causes only a PUC — the mildest level, but still a full CPU restart from the reset vector.
Reset vector address vs reset target 0xFFFE is where the vector is stored; the PC gets the vector's contents. In the simulator, post-PUC PC = 0x4000 (FRAM code start) because _do_reset wipes _memory before _reset_vector_pc() reads it.
WDTHOLD bit vs "any low-byte value" Only bit 7 is WDTHOLD (WDT_HOLD_BIT = 0x80). 0x5A08 is a valid write that leaves the watchdog running. The model tests bool(value & 0x80), nothing else in the low byte.
Wrong password vs missing parameter WDT:PASSWORD 0x1234 → PUC, zero errors. WDT:PASSWORD with no value → ScpiError(-109, "Missing parameter…"), no reset. A malformed command is a SCPI error; a well-formed command carrying a bad password is a hardware event.
INTERRUPT:FLAG? vs INTERRUPT:VECTOR? FLAG? reflects raw pending state (enable ∧ flag) regardless of GIE — like reading an IFG register. VECTOR? is gated by GIE and returns 0x0000 when interrupts are masked, because no maskable interrupt would actually be serviced.
NACK vs SCPI error I2C0:TRANSFER 0x77,"AB" returns the string NACK with zero queued errors — a NACK is a legitimate bus answer ("no device here"), not a protocol violation. Malformed hex (-151) or an out-of-range address (-222) are the command errors.

8. Quiz

Q1. A test sends WDT:PASSWORD 0x5A80. What happens?

  • The write is accepted and the watchdog is held — WDT:STATE? returns HOLD
  • An immediate PUC resets the device
  • SCPI error -109 is queued
  • The write is accepted and the watchdog keeps running

Q2. After CPU:PC 0x8000, GPIO:PORT1:OUTPUT 0xFF, and WDT:STATE HOLD, the test sends WDT:PASSWORD 0x1234. Which assertion set matches test_wrong_password_causes_puc?

  • PC == reset vector, port 1 output == 0x00, wdt.hold is False, errors == 0
  • Only the WDT state resets; PC and GPIO are untouched
  • One SCPI error is queued and the device also resets
  • Nothing — the write is silently accepted as before

Q3. Why does real hardware (and now the model) answer a wrong WDTCTL password with a reset instead of an error code?

  • Runaway code can't be trusted to check errors — a reset halts it immediately and restores a known-good state
  • Resets are faster to execute than setting an error flag
  • WDTCTL is read-only except in a special privileged mode
  • Because the watchdog is disabled during the write, a reset is the only option

Q4. On a fresh device, a test sends I2C0:TRANSFER 0x77,"AB". What comes back, and why?

  • "NACK" — no slave is registered at 0x77, and no SCPI error is queued
  • "00" — transfers behave identically for every address
  • SCPI error -222 (address out of range)
  • A PUC — unknown addresses reset the device

Q5. P1's interrupt enable and flag are both set (bit 0), but no INTERRUPT:GIE ON has been sent. What do INTERRUPT:VECTOR? and INTERRUPT:FLAG? return?

  • VECTOR? → 0x0000, FLAG? → 1
  • VECTOR? → 0x0000, FLAG? → 0
  • VECTOR? → 0xFFDE, FLAG? → 1
  • VECTOR? → 0xFFFF, FLAG? → 0

9. Scenarios — Check Your Understanding

Scenario A: A teammate's SIL test does WDT:STATE HOLD, runs some GPIO setup, then sends WDT:PASSWORD 0xA55A "to re-confirm the hold." Afterwards every GPIO assertion fails with default values and WDT:STATE? says START. They insist "the password command must be broken — 5A is right there in the value!" What actually happened?
Show answer

The password field is bits 15–8 — the upper byte. 0xA55A >> 8 = 0xA5 ≠ 0x5A: the 0x5A they see is in the lower byte, where WDTHOLD and the mode bits live. So the write was a password violation and _do_reset() ran: a full PUC. That explains every symptom at once — GPIO back to defaults (ports rebuilt), wdt.hold back to False (START is the PUC default; the watchdog wakes up running), PC at 0x4000, and — the part that misleads people — an empty error queue, because a PUC is a hardware event, not a SCPI error. (Bonus irony: 0xA5 is the clock system's password, CSCTL0. Right key, wrong lock, and on this register a wrong key reboots the chip.) The fix: WDT:PASSWORD 0x5A80.

Scenario B: You're writing a SIL test for firmware that manages two I2C devices — an EEPROM at 0x50 and a temperature sensor at 0x48 — and must detect when the sensor is missing from the board. Sketch the SCPI/harness sequence for both the "sensor present" and "sensor absent" cases, and predict each transfer's response.
Show answer 
# Sensor PRESENT: place a simulated slave at 0x48 with data to return
inject_i2c_rx(0, b"\x19\x80", address=0x48)   # registers 0x48 + queues rx bytes
I2C0:TRANSFER 0x48,"0000"   → "1980"          # 2 bytes exchanged from 0x48's queue
I2C0:TRANSFER 0x50,"A0"     → "00"            # EEPROM: 0x50 pre-registered, rx empty → zero-fill

# Sensor ABSENT: fresh device, never register 0x48
I2C0:TRANSFER 0x48,"0000"   → "NACK"          # no entry in addr_buffers → bus says no
I2C0:TRANSFER 0x50,"A0"     → "00"            # EEPROM still answers — per-address independence

The key is that addr_buffers gives each address an independent queue, so the missing sensor NACKs while the EEPROM keeps working — exactly what the firmware's "device missing" branch needs to see. Before fa7c595 this test was unwritable: every address returned identical zero-fill from one flat buffer, so present and absent were indistinguishable. Assert firmware handles the NACK without queuing SCPI errors — a NACK is a legitimate answer, not a fault in the test.

Scenario C: A test sets up a pending Timer_A0 interrupt and a pending P1 interrupt, sends INTERRUPT:GIE ON, and asserts INTERRUPT:VECTOR? == "0xFFDE" (P1). It fails with 0xFFE8. Then a colleague "fixes" it by sending WDT:PASSWORD 0x1234 first, and now VECTOR? returns 0x0000 and the test fails differently. Explain both results.
Show answer

First failure — priority. _pending_interrupt_vector() walks _INTERRUPT_PRIORITY = (TB0, TA0, TA1, P1, TA2, P2, …) in Table 9-4 order and returns the first pending source. TA0 (0xFFE8) outranks P1 (0xFFDE), so with both pending, 0xFFE8 is correct — the assertion encoded the wrong expectation, not the model. To see P1's vector, clear or don't set TA0's flag.

Second failure — the PUC wiped everything. WDT:PASSWORD 0x1234 has a wrong password (0x12 ≠ 0x5A), so it ran _do_reset(): both timers' and P1's enable/flag state were rebuilt to defaults and _gie was cleared (SR.GIE is cleared on a PUC, §4.3.3). With GIE clear and nothing pending, VECTOR? returns 0x0000. The "fix" was actually a full reboot sneaking in through the watchdog's password check — a nice demonstration that the PUC path really is shared, and that order matters: reset first, then configure, never the reverse.

input.new_string: // ─── CHANNEL: puc ───────────────────────────────────────────── {id:'p1',ch:'puc',type:'w', q:'Define the three MSP430 reset levels (SLAU367P §1.2), their trigger relationships, and list at least three events that cause ONLY a PUC. Which level does a WDT password violation cause?', c:[{l:'BOR deepest: power-up / supply droop; triggers POR',t:['bor','brownout','power-up','powerup','supply','deepest']}, {l:'POR: caused by BOR / security violation; triggers PUC',t:['por','power-on','power on','security']}, {l:'PUC mildest: WDT expiry, password violations, vacant-memory fetch',t:['puc','power-up clear','mildest','vacant','expiry','password violation']}, {l:'each deeper level triggers the shallower ones',t:['nested','hierarchy','triggers','cascade','implies']}, {l:'WDT password violation → PUC only',t:['only a puc','puc only','just a puc','wdt password violation causes a puc','violation → puc','violation -> puc']}], m:`BOR (brownout reset) — deepest: device power-up, supply falling below the brownout threshold, RST/NMI pin, software PMMSWBOR. A BOR triggers a POR. POR (power-on reset) — middle: caused by a BOR, a security violation, or software PMMSWPOR. A POR triggers a PUC. PUC (power-up clear) — mildest: caused by a POR, plus software-fault events: watchdog expiry in watchdog mode, a WDTCTL password violation, FRAM/CS/PMM register password violations, and instruction fetch from vacant memory. The hierarchy is nested: BOR ⇒ POR ⇒ PUC, never the reverse. Almost every PUC-only source is a symptom of broken software — which is why a WDT password violation causes exactly a PUC: a CPU restart from the reset vector with SR (including GIE) cleared and the watchdog running, without pretending the power failed. Silmulator collapses all three into the single _do_reset path, modeling the consequences rather than the cause machinery.` }, {id:'p2',ch:'puc',type:'mc', q:'After WDT:PASSWORD 0x1234 triggers a PUC, what does errors(mcu) return and why?', opts:[ {t:'0 — a PUC is a hardware event, not a SCPI error; the reset IS the response',c:true, w:'Correct. test_wrong_password_causes_puc asserts errors(mcu) == 0. The handler calls _do_reset() and returns "" without raising. From the client\'s view the command "succeeded" — the evidence is the device state afterwards, exactly like probing real hardware.'}, {t:'1 — the violation queues -224 alongside the reset',c:false,w:'No error is queued. -224 is for illegal parameter VALUES in configuration commands (e.g. WDT:STATE BANANA); a password violation answers with the reset alone.'}, {t:'1 — but the PUC then clears the error queue, so it depends on read order',c:false,w:'Nothing is ever queued: the violation branch is _do_reset() then return "". There is no transient error to race against.'}, {t:'0 — because _do_reset wipes the error queue as part of the reset',c:false,w:'Right count, wrong reason: no error was raised in the first place. The design point is that hardware events and command errors are different channels.'}, ] }, {id:'p3',ch:'puc',type:'mc', q:'Which of these does the shared _do_reset() path NOT do?', snip:`# _do_reset: ports/adc/timers/uart/spi/i2c/clock/pm rebuilt, # wdt = WDTState(), _veref_v = 1.2, _memory = {}, # _pc = _reset_vector_pc(), _registers zeroed, _gie = False`, opts:[ {t:'Preserve FRAM memory contents — the model wipes _memory, though a real PUC does not erase FRAM',c:true, w:'Correct — this is the divergence to remember. _do_reset sets self._memory = {} BEFORE reading the reset vector, so the vector is always unwritten post-PUC and the PC lands at the 0x4000 FRAM-code-start default. Real FRAM survives a PUC.'}, {t:'Reload the PC from the reset vector',c:false,w:'It does: self._pc = self._reset_vector_pc(), matching SLAU367P §1.2/§4.3.'}, {t:'Clear GIE',c:false,w:'It does: self._gie = False with the comment "SR.GIE is cleared on a PUC (SLAU367P §4.3.3)" — added by 615b4e1.'}, {t:'Reset the watchdog to its running (START) default',c:false,w:'It does: self.wdt = WDTState() and WDTState.hold defaults to False — the post-PUC watchdog is ACTIVE, as on silicon.'}, ] }, {id:'p4',ch:'puc',type:'w', q:'Explain "protection by reset": why does WDTCTL answer a wrong password with a PUC instead of an error flag? Frame it in terms of what runaway code can and cannot do.', c:[{l:'watchdog exists to catch runaway code (corrupted PC, wild writes)',t:['runaway','corrupted','wild','garbage','spray']}, {l:'runaway code never checks error flags',t:['never checks','doesn\'t check','ignores error','won\'t read','no one reads']}, {l:'random 16-bit write has 1/256 chance of a valid password',t:['1/256','1 in 256','255/256','random','probabil']}, {l:'wrong write halts execution NOW and restores known-good state',t:['immediately','halts','known-good','known good','reset vector','recovery']}, {l:'error-code design could let random writes eventually disable the dog',t:['eventually','silently disable','keep running','keeps trying','slip through']}], m:`The watchdog is the mechanism that catches runaway code, so it must not be disableable BY runaway code. Runaway code — a corrupted PC executing garbage — looks like a stream of random writes, and it never checks status flags; an error-code design would be invisible to it, and the random stream could keep executing until it happened to write a valid 0x5Axx pattern that stops the dog. Protection by reset closes that hole: any WDTCTL write without 0x5A in the upper byte (255 of 256 random patterns) triggers an immediate PUC. Execution of the runaway code ends right there — PC reloads from the reset vector, peripherals return to defaults, the watchdog restarts. The protection's failure mode is recovery to a known-good state rather than continued execution. Silmulator models this faithfully: _wdt_password calls _do_reset() on a bad upper byte — the same shared path *RST uses — and queues no SCPI error, because the reset is the answer.` }, {id:'p5',ch:'puc',type:'mc', q:'A test sets CPU:PC 0x8000, then triggers a PUC via WDT:PASSWORD 0x0000. Order matters inside _do_reset: self._memory = {} happens before self._pc = self._reset_vector_pc(). With both bytes absent, the function returns 0x4000 (SLASE54D memory map: FRAM code start). test_wrong_password_causes_puc asserts mcu._pc == mcu._reset_vector_pc() — evaluated post-reset, that IS 0x4000.'}, {t:'0xFFFE — the PC jumps to the reset vector\'s address',c:false,w:'0xFFFE is where the vector is STORED. The PC gets the vector\'s CONTENTS (or the 0x4000 default when unwritten). Confusing the pointer with the pointee is the classic reset-vector mistake.'}, {t:'0x8000 — the PC survives because it was set via SCPI, not by firmware',c:false,w:'The PUC resets CPU state regardless of how it was set: _pc is reassigned inside _do_reset. A real MSP430 fetches the reset vector too — it never starts at address 0.'}, ] }, // MORE-BANK

WDTPW password

0x5A in bits 15–8 of every WDTCTL write
Definition
The write password guarding the watchdog control register (SLAU367P §24.2): every 16-bit write to WDTCTL must carry 0x5A in its upper byte or the write is a password violation — punished with an immediate PUC, not an error flag. Reads of WDTCTL return 0x69 in the upper byte on real silicon, so the password is strictly a write credential.
Project example
Commit 5e2ba08 added WDT_PASSWORD = 0x5A and the check in _wdt_password: if (value >> 8) != self.WDT_PASSWORD: self._do_reset(). So WDT:PASSWORD 0x5A80 is accepted (and holds the dog), while 0x1234 — and the byte-swapped 0xA55A — reset the simulated device.
Usage
"Your write has 0x5A in the lower byte — the WDTPW password lives in the upper byte, which is why the device keeps rebooting."
Contrast with: an access-control password
WDTPW is not secret and not authentication — it's printed in the datasheet. It is a statistical guard: intentional code always knows it, while random runaway writes hit it only 1 time in 256. Its job is distinguishing deliberate writes from garbage, not keeping people out.

PUC (power-up clear)

the software-fault reset — SLAU367P §1.2
Definition
The mildest MSP430 reset level. It restarts the CPU — PC loaded from the reset vector at 0xFFFE, SR cleared (GIE = 0), peripherals to reset values, watchdog active — without any power event. Its non-POR causes are all symptoms of broken software: watchdog expiry, password violations on WDTCTL/CS/FRAM/PMM registers, fetch from vacant memory.
Project example
In msp430.py a PUC is self._do_reset() — the same shared path *RST uses: all peripheral state rebuilt, _memory cleared, _pc = self._reset_vector_pc() (0x4000 once memory is wiped), _gie = False. test_wrong_password_causes_puc proves it is device-wide by dirtying PC, GPIO and WDT state and asserting all three are wiped — with errors(mcu) == 0.
Usage
"After the bad WDTCTL write the board isn't hung — it PUCs, runs to the same bad write, and PUCs again: a boot loop."
Contrast with: a SCPI error
A malformed command (missing parameter → -109, bad token → -224) queues an error and changes nothing. A PUC queues nothing and changes everything — it is a hardware event whose evidence is the post-reset state, not the error queue.

BOR/POR/PUC hierarchy

brownout ⇒ power-on ⇒ power-up clear
Definition
The three nested MSP430 reset levels (SLAU367P §1.2). BOR (deepest): power-up, supply droop below the brownout threshold, RST pin. POR: caused by a BOR or a security violation. PUC (mildest): caused by a POR or by software faults. Each deeper level triggers everything below it — a BOR implies a POR implies a PUC, never the reverse.
Project example
Silmulator collapses all three into the single _do_reset() path — the audit's *RST row reads "Restores simulator defaults via the same _do_reset path a WDT password violation PUC uses, including WDTHOLD." The model reproduces PUC consequences (state wiped, PC at the vector, GIE clear, watchdog running) rather than the three-tier cause machinery.
Usage
"A watchdog event only causes a PUC — if your brownout-flag logic expects a BOR after a WDT reset, it will never fire."
Contrast with: a single 'reset' concept
On parts with one reset, "the chip reset" is one fact. On the MSP430 the level carries diagnostic information: firmware reads SYSRSTIV to learn whether it woke from power loss (BOR) or from its own misbehaviour (PUC) — and logs or degrades accordingly.

Watchdog (WDT_A)

the timer that resets you for not talking to it
Definition
A hardware countdown (SLAU367P §24) that triggers a PUC if firmware fails to service ("pet") it before the interval expires. It converts every hang, livelock or runaway into a bounded outage ending in a reset. It powers up running — WDTHOLD = 0 after a PUC — so firmware must stop or service it early in boot.
Project example
Commit 5e2ba08's WDTState dataclass stores hold: bool = False — the PUC default — driven by two doors into one bit: WDT:STATE HOLD|START and the password-gated WDT:PASSWORD write (bit 7, WDT_HOLD_BIT = 0x80). Deliberately absent: WDTIS interval select and expiry — time does not pass in the simulation, so the dog never fires on its own; the families scored PARTIAL, not COMPLIANT.
Usage
"Every MSP430 example starts with WDTCTL = WDTPW | WDTHOLD because the watchdog wakes up running — hold it or pet it within ~32 ms."
Contrast with: an ordinary timer (Timer_A/B)
Timer_A/B count for the application — PWM, capture, periodic interrupts — and are entirely under firmware control. The watchdog counts against the application, behind a password, with a reset as its terminal event. One is a peripheral you use; the other is a supervisor you answer to.

Protection by reset

the failure mode is recovery
Definition
The design pattern where an invalid write to a safety-critical register triggers a reset rather than an error indication. Rationale: the threat is runaway code, and runaway code never checks error flags — but a reset ends its execution immediately and restores a known-good state. The protection cannot be ignored, because it removes the thing that would have to do the ignoring.
Project example
The violation branch of _wdt_password: self._do_reset() # wrong password: immediate PUC — followed by return "", no ScpiError. The pre-5e2ba08 model accepted any write silently, which meant a SIL suite would happily certify firmware whose watchdog write boot-loops real hardware.
Usage
"A corrupted PC spraying writes can't silently disable the watchdog — 255 of 256 password bytes cause a PUC first. That's protection by reset."
Contrast with: protection by rejection (-224/-222)
Configuration registers reject bad values with a queued error and unchanged state — fine, because the writer is a test script that reads errors. Safety registers assume the writer may be garbage code that reads nothing; the response must act on the device, not on a status channel. Same goal — refuse the invalid — opposite delivery.

NACK

not-acknowledge — the bus's right to say no
Definition
On I2C, the addressed device pulls SDA low to ACK each byte; if no device answers the address, the line stays high — a NACK (raising UCNACKIFG on eUSCI_B, SLAU367P §32.3.4). A NACK is a legitimate bus answer meaning "nobody home" or "can't take more," not a protocol error.
Project example
Commit fa7c595 gave the model a real NACK path: I2CState.addr_buffers holds one rx/tx queue per populated address, and _i2c_transfer/_i2c_write return "NACK" when the target has no entry. Probe: I2C0:TRANSFER 0x50,"AB" → "00" (default slave, empty queue) but 0x77 → "NACK" — with zero SCPI errors. Before, every address ACKed identically from one flat buffer.
Usage
"The sensor-missing branch was untestable until the model could NACK — a bus that always ACKs can't simulate an empty socket."
Contrast with: a SCPI error
-222 (address out of range for the 7-/10-bit mode) and -151 (bad hex) are command faults — the test script wrote something malformed. A NACK is an in-band bus outcome for a well-formed transfer: the response string, not the error queue. Firmware must handle NACK; test scripts must not cause -222.

GIE (general interrupt enable)

SR bit 3 — SLAU367P §4.3.3
Definition
The status-register bit that master-gates all maskable interrupts. Set by EINT/__enable_interrupt(), cleared by DINT — and cleared automatically by a PUC and on ISR entry. GIE does not affect flag latching: IFG bits set regardless; GIE only decides whether a pending interrupt gets serviced.
Project example
Commit 615b4e1 made GIE real stored state: self._gie, driven by INTERRUPT:GIE ON|OFF and INTERRUPT:ENABLE/DISABLE, cleared in _do_reset ("SR.GIE is cleared on a PUC"). INTERRUPT:VECTOR? returns 0x0000 while GIE is clear even with P1 pending, but INTERRUPT:FLAG? still reads 1 — the gate and the latch are separate, as on silicon.
Usage
"Your flag is set but the vector reads 0x0000 — did anything send INTERRUPT:GIE ON after the reset cleared it?"
Contrast with: per-source enables (P1IE, TAIE…)
Each source has its own enable bit ANDed with its flag to make it pending; GIE is the single global gate over servicing all of them. The model mirrors both layers: _source_pending() checks enable ∧ flag per source, and only _int_vector applies the GIE gate. NMIs (not modeled) ignore GIE entirely — that's what "maskable" means.

Interrupt vector priority

SLASE54D Table 9-4 — position is precedence
Definition
Every FR5994 interrupt source has a fixed word address in the vector table (0xFF90–0xFFFE) and a fixed priority given by its table position — reset at 0xFFFE is highest. When several sources are pending simultaneously, the highest-priority one is serviced first; the rest stay pending.
Project example
Commit 615b4e1 encodes the real addresses and order for the tracked sources: _TIMERB_VECTOR = 0xFFF4, _TIMERA_VECTORS = {0: 0xFFE8, 1: 0xFFE0, 2: 0xFFDA}, _GPIO_PORT_VECTORS = {1: 0xFFDE, … 8: 0xFFB6}, walked via _INTERRUPT_PRIORITY = ("TB0","TA0","TA1","P1","TA2","P2",…) — timers and ports interleaved exactly as Table 9-4 lists them. With TA0 and P1 both pending, INTERRUPT:VECTOR? answers 0xFFE8, not 0xFFDE.
Usage
"Don't assert the P1 vector while a timer flag is still set — TA0 outranks P1 in Table 9-4, so VECTOR? reports 0xFFE8 first."
Contrast with: the reset vector
The reset vector (0xFFFE) is in the same table but isn't a maskable interrupt: it ignores GIE, tops the priority column, and its "service routine" is the program itself. _pending_interrupt_vector() never returns it — a PUC reaches the reset vector through _do_reset, not through the interrupt query. And 0x0000 is not a vector at all: it's the IV-register idiom for "nothing pending."

Stored as `_gie`; `INTERRUPT:VECTOR?` is GIE-gated (0x0000 while clear) but `INTERRUPT:FLAG?` reports pending state ungated — the gate and the IFG latch are separate, as on silicon. |
